stage1/problem/A1/v1:
Problem: In MVFA's zero-shot (leave-one-modality-out) training, the segmentation adapters — the only part that produces anomaly maps — are trained with Dice and Focal losses exclusively on the three source datasets that have pixel masks (BrainMRI, LiverCT, RESC), while OCT17, ChestXray and HIS only train the detection adapters. Can the segmentation adapters be trained from image-level labels alone? At every one of the four adapter levels, with the original level weights, the Dice and Focal terms are replaced by an image-level BCE on the top-k mean of the level's patch anomaly probabilities (k = 1% of patches: an abnormal image must contain a few strongly abnormal patches, a normal image none), applied to all five source datasets with every mask discarded; the detection adapters and their loss are unchanged. Hypothesis: because the patch scores are similarities to fixed text anchors shared across modalities, this weak supervision yields localisation that transfers to the unseen modality, and it emerges mainly at the deeper adapter levels. Outcomes on the held-out modality: pixel-level AUROC and AUPRO (on the folds with masks: BrainMRI, LiverCT, RESC), image-level AUROC (all folds), and a level-wise breakdown, comparing mask-supervised MVFA with image-label-supervised MVFA trained and model-selected under the shared protocol; a label-budget curve adds variants with masks for only 10% and 25% of the abnormal source images.

Rationale: Limitations L3, L5 and L18, checked against the released code, show that MVFA's localisation depends on dense expert masks from three datasets and that half of the benchmark never teaches the segmentation branch anything; L4 shows the same dependence in the few-shot mode. Image-level labels are cheap and available for every BMAD dataset, yet MVFA never uses them to supervise where anomalies are. The related literature does not answer whether text-anchored patch similarities inside a multi-level CLIP adapter can learn transferable localisation from weak labels: MedSAD-CLIP [40] and MLCA [58] keep pixel-level supervision, MadCLIP [29] and the consistency-margin adapter [54] rely on labelled abnormal images, MediCLIP [22], AnomaMed [53] and the UWF framework [43] replace labels with synthetic anomalies, and image-level supervision has been used for separate generative models [10] rather than for the adapter's own maps. The change is one loss term in the public training script at the original compute budget; a one-fold pilot that monitors the fraction of normal-image patches above 0.5 guards against collapsed maps. Either outcome is informative: success makes MVFA trainable from report-level labels, and failure, together with the label-budget curve, quantifies what masks are worth for cross-modality localisation — the cost that L18 says is never measured.
stage1/problem/A2/v1:
Problem: In MVFA's few-shot mode, the released code defines a K-shot support set as K normal and K abnormal target-domain images, the abnormal ones with expert pixel masks, used to fine-tune the adapters (Dice, Focal and BCE losses), while the memory bank holds the normal supports. Can the K real abnormal images with masks be replaced by synthetic abnormal images built from the K normal supports alone, and does the size of the gap depend on the type of lesion? Synthesis: one synthetic image per normal support and epoch, made by Poisson-blending an elliptical patch (2-15% of the image area) cut from a different normal image of the same modality, with random intensity scaling, the pasted region serving as the mask; the memory bank keeps only real normal supports. Outcomes per BMAD dataset for K in {2, 8} (full range K in {2, 4, 8, 16} on BrainMRI and ChestXray): few-shot image-level AUROC, pixel-level AUROC and AUPRO of the synthetic variant relative to real-abnormal MVFA, with a memory-bank-only variant as the lower reference. Hypothesis: the synthetic variant recovers most of the gain on focal-lesion datasets (BrainMRI, LiverCT, RESC) and little on diffuse-finding datasets (ChestXray, HIS, OCT17).

Rationale: L4 and L18, confirmed in the released code, show that 'K = 4' means four normal plus four expertly delineated abnormal slices, and the paper never measures what those abnormal images contribute. Synthetic anomalies are a known substitute when adapting CLIP to medical images (MediCLIP [22], LesionPaste [32], the UWF framework's Poisson blending [43], AnomaMed [53]), and [55] shows that the choice of synthetic images matters; but none measures the gap to real abnormal supervision inside the same adapter with the same support set, and none asks for which kinds of medical anomaly the substitution fails. The question isolates the abnormal half of the support set, keeps architecture, losses and evaluation unchanged, needs only image operations on BMAD data, and is sized to one GPU; its answer is a decision rule for a new site: when collecting K annotated abnormal cases is worth the expert time.
stage1/problem/B1/v1:
Problem: In MVFA's few-shot inference, the released code min-max normalises the zero-shot (text) branch and the few-shot (memory-bank) branch with the minimum and maximum over the entire test set and adds them with a fixed weight of 0.5, so the score of one image depends on the rest of the test set and a single incoming image cannot be scored. Can this transductive normalisation be replaced by an inductive one computed only from the K normal support images, at a small cost in AUROC? The inductive normaliser maps each branch's patch scores through the 1st and 99th percentiles of the leave-one-out patch scores of the supports (every patch of support i scored against the memory bank of the other K-1 supports and against the text anchors), which gives thousands of reference values even at K = 2; the fusion weight and the max pooling of the image score are kept fixed. Primary outcome: image-level and pixel-level AUROC of inductive versus transductive normalisation on each held-out BMAD dataset for K in {2, 4, 8, 16}. Motivating measurement: the spread of the original method's AUROC across random half-size test subsets and at shifted prevalence (10% and 50% abnormal). Secondary outcome: sensitivity at 95% specificity with a threshold fixed from the support scores alone.

Rationale: The code check turned L10 into a sharper limitation (C1): the fusion is computed with test-set extremes, which makes the method non-deployable on a stream of images and makes its numbers depend on test-set composition; L8 adds that only threshold-free AUROC is reported, so this dependence stays invisible. Related work changes representations, prompts and fusion layers (LaRP-CLIP [57], HeadCLIP [17], ClipMPCAD [62]) but evaluates with the same AUROC; QueCo [56] even builds its reference from the unlabelled test set, while CANOR [30] shows that a few calibration scalars can be fitted cheaply for a frozen CLIP. The study is positioned as an evaluation-validity study with a simple inductive fix: it reuses the K normal supports MVFA already loads, needs no retraining, is confined to test_few.py, and runs on checkpoints retrained under the shared protocol. Keeping the pooling fixed isolates one component, and the inductive normaliser can be adopted by other methods evaluated on BMAD.
stage1/problem/B2/v1:
Problem: MVFA's image score uses different pooling rules in different places — the paper's Eq. 3 takes the maximum over the anomaly map, the released code trains the detection adapters with a mean-pooled map, and inference scores masked datasets by the maximum of the fused segmentation map and unmasked datasets by the mean-pooled detection map. Is the best image-level pooling of the fused segmentation map a function of the typical lesion area of a modality, so that it can be chosen for an unseen modality from the source modalities alone? Candidates: maximum, mean, and top-k mean with k in {0.1%, 1%, 5%, 20%} of the patches, applied to the fused segmentation map on all six datasets. The k chosen on the source modalities' validation split (shared protocol) is compared with the best k in hindsight and with the code's dataset-dependent rule, by image-level AUROC (mean and standard deviation over seeds and support draws) in the zero-shot and few-shot settings. Robustness: the drop in image-level AUROC when one patch of each normal test map is set to the 99.9th percentile of abnormal-image patch scores.

Rationale: L38 and C3 show that one spurious patch can decide an image's label and that the paper and the code disagree on pooling; L30 shows that the scoring pipeline differs between datasets, so the reported detection numbers cannot be attributed to the method as described. Pooling ablations exist in industrial anomaly detection ([12], [15]), and medical CLIP methods add joint or prototype image scores ([17], [57]); CANOR [30] argues that uniform max or mean aggregation ignores how chest X-ray findings combine. What is not known is whether the right pooling transfers across medical modalities whose anomalies range from small focal lesions (BrainMRI, LiverCT) to diffuse changes (ChestXray, HIS). The study is inference-only on retrained checkpoints and needs a few lines in the test scripts; it yields one documented rule and a selection procedure a practitioner can apply to a new modality.
